name: Patricia and radix tries in crawl-state architecture. Aliases: PATRICIA (Practical Algorithm To Retrieve Information Coded In Alphanumeric, Morrison 1968), radix tree, compressed trie, path-compressed trie, crit-bit tree; adjacent named variants ART (Adaptive Radix Tree, Leis et al. 2013), HOT, Judy arrays, Merkle Patricia Trie (Ethereum), and the Linux kernel's XArray/radix tree. In crawl systems the relevant deployments are the crawl frontier and URL-seen set (Mercator, IRLbot DRUM, Frontera, Tree-Frontier), plus the URL prefix and IP-prefix lookups that politeness and robots caching depend on.
kind: Data structure (research result with production implementations), not a standard, benchmark, service or regulation. Evaluated here as an architectural choice for the project's own crawl/ingest state, and as the literature that should explain the project's measured ingest degradation.
maturity: Production and effectively frozen at the algorithm level. Morrison 1968; Sedgewick's radix-search chapter is a standard undergraduate treatment. Active research is in cache-conscious and SIMD-friendly variants (ART 2013, HOT 2018) and in persistent/verifiable variants (Merkle Patricia Trie), not in the base structure. Crawl-frontier engineering literature (Mercator 1999, IRLbot 2008, UbiCrawler, Frontera) is mature and largely unchanged; the recent work is Tree-Frontier style sampling for focused crawling (arXiv 2112.07620), which is a policy layer over the same storage.
license: The algorithm is unencumbered public academic work. Implementations vary: Linux XArray is GPL-2.0 (not usable here), the common Python/Rust/C libraries are permissive (datrie MIT-ish, pygtrie Apache-2.0, Rust radix_trie MIT/Apache-2.0, ART reference code BSD/MIT-family). Nothing blocks use in this project; the project already implements its own trie, so licence is only relevant if a library is vendored. [uncertain] on the exact licence of any specific implementation the project might adopt.
keeps_and_discards: A patricia trie keeps exactly the key set and whatever payload is hung off nodes; it discards nothing about the keys and asserts nothing about the values. Path compression collapses single-child chains into edge labels, so the structure keeps every distinguishing character of every key while storing shared prefixes once. What it discards is any notion of similarity that is not prefix similarity: two keys that differ in the first character share nothing, regardless of how similar the rest is. For a key of the shape url : xpath : markdown : content this is a strong and mostly favourable property -- all nodes of one page share the url prefix and all siblings share the xpath prefix, so the store is compressed exactly along the axis the project cares about -- but it also means the trie gives zero help with cross-origin dedup, because the url component is the highest-order field and two identical fragments on two origins land in disjoint subtrees. The standard crawl-state instantiation makes the same tradeoff deliberately: URLs are stored reversed-host-first (com.example/path) precisely so that prefix compression aligns with the politeness and partitioning axis rather than with the lexical accident of the scheme. If the project wants cross-origin dedup it needs a second, content-keyed index; the trie alone will not supply it, and the dedup-storage literature is explicit that the content-keyed index is the part that does not compress and does not stay in cache.
structure_preserved: Nesting and order are preserved exactly and cheaply: the trie IS the nesting, and an in-order traversal of a radix trie over xpath-shaped keys reproduces document order provided sibling indices are zero-padded or otherwise made lexicographically monotone. This is a real and frequently-missed implementation detail -- div[2] sorts before div[10] lexicographically only if the index is padded, so an unpadded xpath key silently reorders siblings past the ninth. Tabular relations are not preserved except as sibling adjacency; a table is a subtree and the row/column relation has to be recovered from the xpath step names. Shadow boundaries are preserved if and only if the key encoding makes the boundary an explicit step (e.g. a distinguished separator or a shadow-depth field in the address); if shadow content is flattened into the composed-tree xpath with no marker, the boundary is destroyed and cannot be recovered from the key. The Ethereum Merkle Patricia Trie is the reference for the stronger form: hashing each node makes the structure itself verifiable and gives O(log n) proof of membership, which is the mechanism worth borrowing if the project ever needs to prove that a stored capture was not edited.
interactive_elements: Not addressed by the structure. Controls appear only as whatever the key encoding and payload record about them. The relevant design point is that a trie can carry interactivity in the key (an 'interactive' bit or a role token appended to the xpath step) at effectively zero cost, because the bit lives inside the already-stored path label. This is the cheapest possible place to put the project's tag-plus-interactivity signal, and it keeps that signal out of the payload where it would otherwise be duplicated per capture.
interactive_state_fidelity: Nothing intrinsic. Disabled/checked/selected/expanded/aria states must be stored as node payload, and payload is exactly the part that does not compress. This matters more than it appears: state fields are high-churn (checked flips on every click) while the address is stable, so storing state in the payload of a stable node means every state change rewrites a node, whereas storing state in the KEY means every state change creates a new node and permanently grows the trie. The project should store address in the key and state in a versioned payload cell, otherwise a page with a live clock or a hovered menu grows the key space without bound. Token cost of carrying state at all is low if it is emitted as a compact suffix on the element line rather than as a separate attributes block; the accessibility tree's advantage over markdown is that it carries these states by default, and the trie's advantage over the AX tree is that it can carry them without also carrying the AX tree's computed-name machinery.
layout_awareness: None, and this is the structure's cleanest fit with the project's no_layout_in_the_fold constraint. A trie keyed on address is geometry-free by construction. Geometry can be attached as a side table keyed by the same address, which is precisely the 'peripheral keyed by address' the project specifies -- the trie supplies the join key for free, and an actuator reading geometry does a point lookup, never a scan. Nothing in the crawl-state literature reads layout; the frontier is a URL structure.
javascript_required: Not applicable to the structure itself. Relevant only in that the crawl-frontier literature that matters here (Mercator, IRLbot) is pre-JavaScript and assumes a fetch-parse-extract loop over static HTML; its cost models therefore do not account for a live rendered page, and its dedup assumptions (URL-seen, shingle-seen) assume a document arrives once and is finished. A live composed shadow DOM under mutation violates that assumption, which is the main reason the crawl-state literature's numbers should not be transferred to this project without re-measurement.
evaluation_method: For the structure itself: asymptotic analysis (O(k) lookup in key length k, independent of n) plus cache-miss counting on modern variants. The ART paper's evaluation method is the standard modern one -- measure lookups/second and cache misses against B+-tree and hash table baselines at several dataset sizes on one machine. The probabilistic analysis of Ethereum's Patricia trie (arXiv 2408.14217) combines an analytic depth model with empirical validation against real chain state, which is the closest published thing to 'does the trie behave as advertised on real, adversarially-shaped keys'. For crawl frontiers: throughput at scale (IRLbot reports crawl rate and URL-seen throughput on a single machine over a 6.3 billion page crawl), and DRUM's explicit design target is bounded disk I/O per URL check as the seen-set exceeds RAM. Method quality is generally good for throughput and poor for degradation-over-time, which is the project's actual question -- almost no published evaluation plots per-operation latency against store size on identical repeated inputs, which is exactly the measurement the project has and the literature does not.
corpus_size_and_origins: Wildly heterogeneous and mostly not web-shaped. ART and HOT evaluate on synthetic integer keys, sparse/dense uniform distributions, and a handful of string sets (typically a URL list and a dictionary of a few million entries). IRLbot's crawl is 6.3 billion pages from ~117 million hosts (2007), which is the only genuinely large, genuinely multi-origin evaluation in the crawl-frontier line, and it is nearly two decades old and pre-JavaScript. The Ethereum trie analysis uses real mainnet state (hundreds of millions of accounts) but the keys are 256-bit hashes, i.e. uniformly random -- the opposite of the project's highly structured, heavily shared-prefix keys, so its depth distributions do not transfer. Nothing in this literature is evaluated on a corpus resembling 136 pages from 109 origins with per-node xpath keys; the project's own corpus is the only evidence for the project's own key shape.
reported_precision_recall: Not a precision/recall structure; no such figures exist and any quoted would be category error. The transferable published numbers are performance figures: ART reports roughly an order-of-magnitude lookup advantage over a red-black tree and parity-to-better against a hash table while retaining order, measured on synthetic keys by its own authors; IRLbot reports a sustained ~1,789 pages/s average crawl rate on one machine with the URL-seen set on disk; RocksDB issue 13981 and the MatrixKV paper (USENIX ATC 2020) document the contrasting LSM behaviour -- write amplification rising with tree depth, and performance deteriorating markedly once the store reaches large sizes (MatrixKV frames the problem as all-to-all compaction consuming CPU and device bandwidth, producing write stalls and long-tail latency). Those LSM numbers are the ones that bear on the project's 582 -> 840 -> 1539 ms degradation, not the trie numbers.
independent_oracle: For the structure: yes and it is strong -- a trie's correctness is checkable by an oracle that shares no assumptions with it, namely a hash map or sorted list holding the same key set, compared for identical membership and identical ordered enumeration. This is cheap, exhaustive, and the project should run it as a permanent invariant. For the performance question there is no independent oracle in the literature at all; every published number is the authors' own single-machine measurement, and there is no cross-implementation benchmark suite for crawl frontiers comparable to what exists for key-value stores (YCSB, db_bench), so cross-paper comparisons are not sound.
evidence_independence: Almost entirely author-run or vendor-run. ART's numbers are by its authors; MatrixKV's are by its authors against RocksDB configured by them; the RocksDB universal-compaction degradation report is a user-filed issue, which is genuinely independent of the RocksDB authors but is a single uncontrolled workload. The Ethereum trie paper is independent of the Ethereum client teams and is one of the few third-party validations of a deployed trie's real behaviour. Practitioner reports on B-tree insert degradation (the SQLite forum threads, the voidstar.tech insert-speed measurements, the widely circulated 'random UUID made your inserts 10x slower' write-up) are independent of SQLite's authors but are uncontrolled blog-grade measurements and should be treated as hypothesis sources, not as figures. Nothing here should be laundered into the record as a measured cross-system comparison.
page_archetype_coverage: Not measured, and there is a real archetype effect the literature ignores. Key-space shape varies enormously by archetype: a documentation page produces a deep, narrow, highly prefix-shared xpath set that compresses beautifully; a listing or collection page produces thousands of near-identical sibling subtrees that differ only in a numeric index, which is the worst case for path compression because each sibling forks at a single character deep in the key and every fork allocates a node; a forum page interleaves both. A product page with a virtualised list is worse still, because scrolling re-creates the same content under different indices, inflating the key space without adding information. Any claim that the trie 'compresses the corpus by X' is archetype-dependent and should be reported per archetype, mirroring the reason WCXB's 0.93-to-0.41 spread makes aggregates misleading.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Script-invariant if and only if the key is byte- or codepoint-keyed over a normalised encoding. This is the sharp edge. A byte-keyed radix trie over UTF-8 branches mid-codepoint, which is harmless for lookup but makes edge labels meaningless to inspect and makes any prefix-based aggregation wrong for non-ASCII. A codepoint-keyed trie is safe but wider. Worse, unnormalised Unicode makes the trie non-deterministic across sources: the same visible xpath step name or content in NFC and NFD produces two distinct keys, so a store fed by two different serialisers silently double-counts. The project must pin a normalisation form (NFC is the web default and what the DOM's own comparisons assume) and must apply it identically at write and at query. CJK and RTL raise no structural problem for the trie; RTL raises a display problem in the ASCII wireframe, which is an actuator concern. Whitespace-free segmentation is irrelevant to the address key and highly relevant to any content-keyed sibling index, where shingling assumptions break.
leaks_outward: Nothing. A trie is an in-process data structure; it makes no network calls and is invisible to the page. The crawl-frontier layer above it does leak -- fetch order, request timing, and the very fact of following a link are all observable to the origin -- but that is the crawler's behaviour, not the structure's. Worth noting for the project: a frontier that expands nodes in strict prefix order produces a highly recognisable request pattern (all of one host, in lexical path order), which is a fingerprintable crawl signature; randomised or politeness-shuffled dequeue is the standard mitigation and costs nothing structurally.
mechanism_detectability: Zero for the structure. The trie cannot be detected by a page because it never touches the page. This is one of the few items in this set with no detectability surface at all, and it is worth stating plainly because it means all detectability risk in the project's ingest path lives in the browser-side sensor, not in the store.
countermeasures: Not applicable defensively. The hardening that matters is against the store's own pathologies rather than against an adversary: bound key length (a maliciously deep DOM produces unbounded xpath strings and therefore unbounded trie depth -- a page can inflate the key space arbitrarily by nesting divs, which is a cheap denial-of-service against the ingest path), reject or truncate keys past a depth cap and record the truncation, and cap sibling index width so a page with a million list items cannot exhaust the node arena. IRLbot's DRUM design exists precisely because adversarial and machine-generated URL spaces (infinite calendars, session-id explosions) overwhelm naive seen-sets; the equivalent hazard here is an infinite or generated DOM.
measured_fidelity_cost: None -- the structure is lossless with respect to its key set, so there is no fidelity/hardening tradeoff to measure. The only cost of the defensive caps above is the fidelity lost to truncation, which is measurable directly as the count and identity of truncated addresses, and which should be recorded as a per-capture field rather than asserted to be rare.
gate_state_at_capture: Not represented unless the key or payload carries it. The recommendation follows directly from the trie's own shape: gate state (consent banner present, paywalled, logged-in, CAPTCHA interposed) belongs in the url-level node's payload, where it is stored once per capture rather than once per node, and where it is automatically inherited by every descendant address at query time by walking to the root. That is a free capability the trie gives and a flat store does not, and it is the cheapest available fix for the corpus-mixing problem that the 67%-of-top-sites consent-interface figure implies.
determinism: Deterministic given a fixed key set and a canonical key encoding. Two caveats that bite in practice. First, iteration order over children must be defined; a hash-bucketed child map (common in ART-style implementations and in naive dict-of-children Python tries) enumerates children in an order that is stable within a process but not across processes if hash randomisation is on, so serialising the trie without an explicit sort produces byte-different output run to run. Second, insertion order must not affect structure -- for a pure patricia trie it does not, which is a genuine advantage over a B-tree or LSM store whose on-disk layout depends on arrival order and on compaction timing. That property makes the trie a good basis for a reproducible artifact: the serialised form can be made a canonical function of the key set alone.
determinism_across_versions: Structure-stable across versions of the implementation, but the KEY is not stable across browser versions, and that is where drift enters. An xpath depends on the parsed DOM, and browser parsers change: whitespace text nodes, implied tbody insertion, template and slot handling, and error-recovery for malformed markup have all changed across Chromium releases. The same page captured under two browser versions can therefore produce different xpath addresses for the same visible element, which the trie will faithfully record as two different nodes. This is a real reproducibility hazard and the mitigation is to record the browser build in the capture metadata and treat cross-build comparisons as suspect until re-anchored. Serialisation format drift (node arena layout, varint encoding) affects only the on-disk artifact and is controllable by versioning the format explicitly.
reproducibility: High for the structure, contingent for the corpus. Re-running ingest over the same stored inputs reproduces the same trie exactly. Re-running over the same URLs does not, because 75% of the project's own corpus fetches live resources on every read -- the trie will faithfully record a different key set and the difference will be indistinguishable from a code change. The fix is standard and is the WARC-style one: freeze the corpus by storing the fetched bytes and replaying them, and keep the live-fetch path only for drift measurement. Without that, no ingest-performance regression test is trustworthy, including the degradation measurement that motivates this item.
failure_modes: Five that matter here. (1) Key-space explosion from generated or virtualised DOM -- the crawl analogue is the infinite-calendar trap and it is well documented from IRLbot onward. (2) Depth blowup from long keys, since patricia lookup is O(k) in key length and xpath keys grow with DOM depth; deeply nested pages degrade lookup linearly in a way that is invisible in an average-case benchmark. (3) Node-count-driven allocator and garbage-collector pressure, discussed under scale_limits, which is the failure mode the project is most likely actually hitting. (4) Sibling-order corruption from unpadded numeric xpath indices, which is silent and produces wrong document order past index 9. (5) Unicode normalisation mismatch producing duplicate subtrees for the same element. Note that none of (3), (4) or (5) throws; all three degrade or corrupt quietly.
failure_visibility: Mostly silent, which is the wrong side of this project's stated preference. Key-space explosion shows up as memory growth and slowdown, not as an error. Order corruption shows up as wrong output. Normalisation mismatch shows up as inflated node counts. The available loud signals must be added deliberately: assert monotone document order against an independent DOM-order oracle on every capture, assert node count against a ceiling derived from the element count, and assert that the trie's key set equals a hash-set oracle's. All three are cheap and all three convert a silent failure into a hard one, matching the project's no-silent-degradation stance.
scale_limits: This is the field that bears directly on the measured 582 -> 840 -> 1539 ms degradation on identical repeated pages, and the literature does have a name for the general shape even if not for this exact instance. Three candidate mechanisms, all of which grow with store size rather than page size and all of which are largely invisible to a call profiler. (a) TRACING-GC COST PROPORTIONAL TO LIVE OBJECT COUNT. A trie built from Python objects presents one container per node; CPython's cyclic collector's full-collection cost is proportional to the number of tracked container objects, and full collections are triggered by allocation counts, so as the store grows the per-page GC tax rises even though per-page allocation is constant. cProfile attributes GC time to whatever Python frame happened to be executing, and because collections fire at allocation boundaries spread thinly across the whole run, that time smears across thousands of frames and appears as unattributed wall-clock overhead -- which matches the reported ~6% attribution precisely. The standard remedies are gc.freeze() after bulk load (moves already-live objects to a permanent generation and excludes them from subsequent full collections), raising gen-2 thresholds or disabling automatic collection during ingest and collecting on an explicit schedule, and removing Python container objects from the hot path entirely by storing the trie as parallel arrays or in a native/arena representation so node count no longer equals tracked-object count. This is the first hypothesis to test because it is cheap to falsify: run the same ingest with gc.disable() or gc.freeze() and see whether the slope flattens. (b) LSM/B-TREE WRITE AMPLIFICATION AND WRITE STALLS in whatever persistent store backs the trie. The LSM literature is unambiguous that write amplification rises with tree depth, that deeper trees follow from larger datasets, and that when the write rate outruns compaction the store stalls foreground writes outright (MatrixKV, USENIX ATC 2020; the RocksDB universal-compaction degradation report; the ecoTune compaction-policy work, SIGMOD 2025). The B-tree analogue is page-split thrashing under randomly ordered key insertion once the modified working set exceeds the page cache -- the effect the SQLite practitioner reports describe as a roughly 10x insert slowdown caused purely by switching from sequential to random keys. Both are kernel- and native-side and both are close to invisible to cProfile, which only attributes to Python frames. If the store is a native embedded database, time inside a single C entry point is attributed to that call, so the ~6% figure argues against this unless the writes happen on a background thread or in a separate process -- but background compaction threads are exactly how LSM stores work, and time on a compaction thread is invisible to a single-threaded profiler. (c) OS PAGE-CACHE AND mmap FAULT COST. Once the store exceeds resident memory, each write touches pages that must be faulted in; the fault time is kernel time attributed to no Python frame. The dedup-storage literature's canonical statement of this is the disk-bottleneck problem: fingerprints are randomly distributed so index lookups have no locality, and once the index exceeds RAM each lookup costs an I/O. The standard remedies there are directly transferable -- an in-memory Bloom/summary filter to answer negative lookups without touching disk, and stream-informed locality-preserving caching so that related lookups hit the same prefetched block (Zhu et al., Avoiding the Disk Bottleneck in the Data Domain Deduplication File System; sparse indexing and the destor platform's implementations of Extreme Binning, SiLo and Sample Index are the follow-ons). DIAGNOSIS ORDER for the project: measure RSS and gc.get_stats() per page alongside latency, since (a) predicts live-object count and gen-2 collection count rising in step with latency while RSS grows smoothly; run with gc.freeze() to falsify (a) in one experiment; then use an OS-level profiler that samples all threads and kernel time (py-spy with --native and --idle, or perf) rather than cProfile, since the stated symptom -- most wall time attributable to nothing reachable from Python -- is the defining signature of work happening off the Python call graph.
delta_cost_model: A patricia trie's per-change cost is genuinely bounded for the operations it defines: inserting or deleting one key is O(k) in key length with O(1) node allocations (an insert splits at most one edge, creating at most two nodes), independent of the number of keys already stored. That is the strongest O(delta) guarantee in this item set. What falls OUTSIDE that per-change cost, and must be named for the guarantee to be falsifiable: (1) garbage collection and allocator work, whose cost is proportional to total live nodes, not to the change -- this is the leading suspect for the project's measured degradation and it is a genuine violation of O(delta) at the process level even though the data structure is O(delta) at the algorithm level; (2) persistence, where any LSM or B-tree backing store amortises but does not bound per-write cost -- compaction and page splits are batched work proportional to store size that is merely deferred, so an O(delta) claim holds per-operation and fails per-second; (3) rehydration or deserialisation of a subtree that has been paged out, which is proportional to subtree size and can be triggered by a single-node update; (4) any secondary index maintained alongside the trie -- a content-hash index, an embedding index, or a full-text index -- none of which inherit the trie's bound, and an embedding index in particular is O(1) inserts but with a large constant and periodic O(n) reindexing; (5) subtree deletion, which is O(size of subtree) not O(1), so a single DOM mutation that removes a container is a delta of one at the DOM level and a delta of thousands at the trie level -- this is the most important practical exception, because MutationObserver reports a removed subtree as one record and the trie must then walk it; (6) key-prefix change, i.e. anything that renames an ancestor address (an element inserted above a subtree shifts every descendant's xpath index) turns a one-element mutation into an O(subtree) rekey, which is the single largest structural argument for not keying on positional xpath alone.
reanchoring_stability: Poor if the key is a raw positional xpath, and this is the project's stated open problem. A patricia trie amplifies xpath fragility rather than mitigating it: an inserted sibling shifts every following sibling's index, which changes the key prefix for every descendant, which in a prefix-compressed structure means a whole subtree relocates and appears as a mass delete plus a mass insert. There is no measured re-anchor rate for xpath keys in the crawl-state literature -- the frontier literature re-anchors on URLs, which are externally assigned and stable, so it never confronted the problem. The mitigations the structure itself offers are worth taking: because the trie stores every node's content anyway, a content hash can be carried as node payload at negligible cost and used as a secondary key, giving an exact-match-first re-anchor that is deterministic and bounded (hash equal -> re-anchor, hash unequal -> record a miss) with no fuzzy matching and therefore no reproducibility contamination. A second, stronger option borrowed from Merkle Patricia Tries is to hash each node over (child hashes, own content), which makes an unchanged subtree detectable by a single root-hash comparison -- an O(1) test for 'nothing below here changed' that turns re-anchoring of stable regions into one comparison rather than a walk. That is the single most valuable transferable mechanism in this item.
adversarial_exposure: The trie preserves everything, including everything invisible to a human, because it applies no content policy. Hidden elements, off-screen text, zero-size nodes and aria-hidden subtrees all get addresses and all get stored. Whether that exposure reaches a model depends entirely on the projection, not the store, and keeping the store maximal while filtering at projection time is the right split -- it preserves the ability to audit what was concealed, which a filtering store destroys. Without geometry the trie cannot distinguish a rendered paragraph from a display:none one, so it is structurally blind to the largest single concealment class. What it CAN do without geometry is carry the signals that make concealment detectable downstream: inline style and class attribute presence, aria-hidden, hidden attribute, tabindex=-1, and the Unicode composition of the content string. Those are DOM-level and character-level facts, available in the fold, and they bound what a layout-blind design can defend. A separate and underrated exposure: the trie's key space is attacker-controllable, so a hostile page can inflate ingest cost or force key collisions by generating adversarial nesting -- a resource attack rather than a content attack, and one the crawl-frontier literature has fought since the infinite-calendar era.
provenance_carrying: Excellent, and this is the trie's strongest safety property. The key url : xpath : markdown : content already contains origin and address; capture time and gate state attach at the url node and are inherited by walking to the root; shadow depth attaches as a key field. Every stored token therefore has a derivable, exact, non-heuristic provenance path with no additional storage -- the address IS the provenance. This is precisely what the provenance-tagging injection defences require as input and normally have to bolt on. The one thing to get right is that provenance must survive the projection: if the markdown emitted to a model does not carry a stable back-reference to the node address, the provenance exists in the store and not in the artifact the model sees, which defeats the purpose. A compact per-line or per-block address token, or a side-channel map from output offsets to addresses, is the minimum.
roundtrip_safety: Serialise -> parse -> serialise is a fixed point for the trie itself if and only if child iteration order is canonicalised (sorted by edge label as bytes) and the encoding is versioned; without that, round-trip stability is accidental. This should be a permanent test: build, serialise, parse, serialise, assert byte equality, and separately assert that the parsed trie's key set equals the original's under a hash-set oracle. That pair of checks is an oracle-free correctness metric for the whole store and costs nothing. Escaping policy matters at the key level: the separator characters in url : xpath : markdown : content must be escaped inside components or the key is ambiguous, and an unescaped colon in a URL query string is the obvious first bug. Use a length-prefixed or unambiguously escaped composite key rather than a delimiter-joined string.
token_budget_and_ordering: The trie does not emit tokens; it determines what CAN be emitted and in what order, which is the more useful contribution. Two properties matter. First, a trie gives cheap subtree size and subtree token-count aggregates if each node caches the sum of its descendants' costs -- an O(depth) update per insert, well within the delta budget -- and that turns budget allocation into a top-down knapsack over children rather than a truncation of a flat serialisation. This is exactly the mechanism the project's 'pay for a node's child list, not the page' design needs, and it is the reason the trie is the right structure for a budgeted text(budget=...) call: the child list is bounded and its cost is known before it is emitted. Second, ordering: because a trie enumerates in key order, the default emission is document order, and any other order (by size, by interactivity density, by recency of change) requires a secondary sort that the trie can support via cached per-node aggregates. Given the position-bias findings that make ordering an output contract, the recommendation is that a budgeted emission should not simply truncate in document order -- it should emit a complete child list at every level it descends and truncate by DEPTH, so the model always sees a structurally complete frame with explicit elision markers rather than a page that stops mid-sentence.
representation_cost: The trie's own overhead is per-node, not per-page: a compressed node is an edge label plus a child map, and for xpath-shaped keys the shared-prefix compression is very high -- the url and the ancestor path are stored once for an entire page. Rough shape rather than a measured figure: node count is proportional to distinct addresses, which for a typical page is the element count plus text nodes, and the payload dominates the structure once content is stored. The cost that actually matters is the per-node Python object overhead if nodes are Python objects, which is on the order of tens to low hundreds of bytes each before payload and is the multiplier behind both memory growth and GC cost. What is lost per token saved: nothing at the store level, because the trie is lossless; all loss happens in projection. [uncertain] on any specific bytes-per-node or tokens-per-page figure, which should be measured on the project's own corpus rather than cited.
what_could_be_adopted: Four concrete mechanisms. (1) MERKLE NODE HASHING over (own content, ordered child hashes), borrowed from the Ethereum Patricia trie. One root-hash comparison proves a subtree is unchanged, turning re-anchoring and change detection of stable regions into O(1) instead of a walk, and giving tamper-evidence over stored captures for free. This is the highest-value item. (2) CACHED SUBTREE AGGREGATES (descendant count, byte count, token estimate, changed-since-timestamp) maintained on the O(depth) insert path, which is what makes a budgeted top-down expansion possible and what lets the model be told the cost of a child list before paying for it. (3) The DEDUP DISK-BOTTLENECK REMEDIES -- an in-memory summary Bloom filter to answer negative content-hash lookups without I/O, and locality-preserving caching so related lookups share a prefetched block. These are the standard answers to exactly the shape of degradation the project measured, if the degradation turns out to be I/O rather than GC. (4) The DRUM/IRLbot DISCIPLINE of batching seen-set checks and bounding disk I/O per check, plus its hard-won defences against generated key spaces, which map directly onto the generated-DOM hazard. Explicitly NOT worth adopting: the crawl-frontier politeness and prioritisation machinery, which solves a problem the project does not have.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS. A trie assigns no meaning to any key; it never names a region nav or article and cannot. Path compression is a lossless encoding, not a heuristic. The only care needed is that cached per-node aggregates stay purely structural (counts, sizes, hashes) and never become learned or hand-tuned region scores. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, and actively supportive -- the trie is geometry-free and supplies exactly the address key that a geometry peripheral should be keyed by, so the ASCII wireframe's actuator can join to it without geometry ever entering the fold. o_delta: ADOPTABLE AS-IS AT THE ALGORITHM LEVEL, WITH NAMED EXCEPTIONS. Insert and delete of a single key are O(key length) with O(1) allocations. The exceptions listed in delta_cost_model are real and must be stated alongside any O(delta) claim: subtree deletion is O(subtree), ancestor-index shift is O(subtree) rekey, persistence amortises rather than bounds, secondary indices do not inherit the bound, and process-level GC cost scales with total live nodes rather than with the delta. The last is the one that can turn an algorithmically O(delta) system into an empirically superlinear one, and the project's own measurements are consistent with it. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- nothing about the structure requires or encourages a stub, and the hash-set oracle described under independent_oracle is a real check, not a mock. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, no interaction; the trie stores whatever the sensor legitimately obtained and has no opinion about how. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is, and the crawl-frontier literature specifically is NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY -- its cost models predate JavaScript and assume documents arrive once and are final, so its throughput figures should not be transferred, while its failure catalogue (generated key spaces, seen-set exceeding RAM, adversarial URL explosion) transfers well.
governance_signal_handling: The structure handles none of it, but it is the natural place to STORE it. robots.txt rules, Content Signals directives, ai.txt terms, AIPREF vocabulary values and any HTTP 402 or Web Bot Auth outcome are all origin- or path-scoped, which is to say they are prefix-scoped, which is exactly what a radix trie indexes. Storing governance state on the url-prefix path means a policy lookup for any address is a single walk that naturally resolves the most specific matching rule -- the same longest-prefix-match the structure was designed for, and the same mechanism robots.txt path matching already specifies. Crawl frontiers have always done this (robots caching keyed by host is the canonical patricia-trie use in a crawler). Adopting it means a governance decision is never re-fetched or re-parsed per page, and every stored node can answer 'what was I permitted to do with this' from its own address.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The structure is neutral but its properties are unusually favourable under a regime that treats persistent storage of page content as the regulated act. Three points. First, a trie makes ERASURE tractable in a way a flat log does not: a deletion request scoped to an origin or a path prefix is a single subtree removal, and prefix-scoped deletion is the natural operation of the structure -- this is a genuine data-protection advantage worth stating explicitly. Second, because the address is the provenance, a stored fragment can always be traced to the URL and capture time it came from, which is what any lawful-basis record or data-subject response requires. Third, the trie stores whatever the sensor captured, including personal data appearing in page content, form values, and logged-in views; the gate_state field at the url node is what distinguishes a public capture from a behind-login one, and behind-login captures are the ones most likely to contain third-party personal data with no plausible legitimate-interest cover. Recommendation: make gate state and a retention class mandatory fields on the url node, and make prefix-scoped purge a first-class operation with a test. [uncertain] on the specific requirements of EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 as they apply here -- that is item 19's question, and the assessment above is structural, not legal advice.
